title: Importing Fuzzing Coverage Metrics into Formal Spec Completeness Evaluation

original_idea.body:
# Importing Fuzzing Coverage Metrics into Formal Spec Completeness Evaluation

**Problem:** Fuzzing generates coverage metrics (branch coverage, edge coverage) that indicate which program behaviors are tested. These coverage concepts could be imported into formal verification to measure spec completeness, but this transfer has not been done.

**Direction:** For 30 programs, generate formal Lean 4 specs using LLMs. Then run AFL++ fuzzing to generate a coverage map. Measure whether program behaviors NOT covered by the formal spec (branches not captured by theorems) correspond to vulnerabilities or bugs found by the fuzzer.

**Why it matters:** Fuzzing coverage is cheap to compute and well-understood. If fuzzing coverage gaps predict formal spec gaps, combining both tools creates a stronger safety assurance than either alone.

**Relevant context:** KLEE (symbolic execution) and AFL++ (fuzzing) are standard verification tools. Lean 4 proof coverage is not a defined concept. Importing fuzzing coverage as a proxy for spec coverage is a novel cross-domain transfer.

title: Importing Cryptographic Protocol Verification Techniques into AI Behavioral Safety

original_idea.body:
# Importing Cryptographic Protocol Verification Techniques into AI Behavioral Safety

**Problem:** Cryptographic protocol verifiers (ProVerif, Tamarin) can prove that protocols satisfy secrecy and authentication properties under adversarial models. Similar trace-based reasoning could verify behavioral properties of AI agents but this transfer has not been attempted.

**Direction:** Select 5 simple AI agent interaction scenarios (agent + tool calls + environment). Model them as protocol traces in ProVerif notation. Attempt to prove that the agent trace satisfies a behavioral property (e.g., never calls a destructive tool without authorization). Measure what properties can/cannot be expressed.

**Why it matters:** If cryptographic protocol verification frameworks can express AI agent behavioral constraints, they provide a well-studied formal foundation for AI agent safety verification. This is a novel application of mature cryptographic tooling.

**Relevant context:** ProVerif and Tamarin are standard tools for protocol verification. AI agent safety verification is nascent. The Boole framework (CSLib) aims for verification condition generation but does not draw on protocol verification. This is a genuine cross-domain transfer.

title: Applying Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) to LLM-Guided Proof Search

original_idea.body:
# Applying Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) to LLM-Guided Proof Search

**Problem:** Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement (CEGAR) is a powerful technique in model checking that automatically refines abstract models when counterexamples are found. This iterative refinement paradigm could improve LLM proof search but has not been applied.

**Direction:** Implement a CEGAR-inspired Lean 4 proof search: LLM generates abstract proof sketch, Lean checker finds counterexample to sketch, LLM refines. Compare to standard iterative correction (error feedback only) on 30 VeriBench tasks. Measure iterations to success.

**Why it matters:** CEGAR is provably complete for finite systems and empirically efficient. Importing it into LLM proof search could provide more principled convergence guarantees than the current ad-hoc self-correction approach.

**Relevant context:** CEGAR is used in tools like SLAM, BLAST, and CPAchecker. LLM proof search uses unstructured self-correction. This is the first proposal to import CEGAR's structure into LLM-based Lean proof generation.

title: Importing Differential Privacy Proofs into AI Model Verification: Can Formal Privacy Guarantees Be Machine-Checked?

original_idea.body:
# Importing Differential Privacy Proofs into AI Model Verification: Can Formal Privacy Guarantees Be Machine-Checked?

**Problem:** Differential privacy proofs are often manually written and error-prone. Lean 4 and Coq have been used for formal DP proofs (e.g., SampCert). Whether LLMs can generate formal DP proofs for AI training pipelines is unexplored.

**Direction:** Select 10 simple differential privacy mechanisms (Laplace, Gaussian, exponential). Use LLMs to generate Lean 4 or Coq proofs that the mechanism satisfies (ε, δ)-DP. Compare to reference proofs in SampCert. Measure LLM success rate and characterize where DP proofs are harder than general functional proofs.

**Why it matters:** Formally verified differential privacy would give cryptographically rigorous privacy guarantees for AI training data. This cross-domain transfer bridges AI privacy and formal verification.

**Relevant context:** SampCert is a Lean 4 library for formally verified DP (Amazon Web Services). DP proofs are mathematically non-trivial. This is a concrete, scoped application of LLM-assisted formal verification to AI safety.

title: Importing Type Theory Guarantees from Dependent Types into LLM Output Validation

original_idea.body:
# Importing Type Theory Guarantees from Dependent Types into LLM Output Validation

**Problem:** Dependently typed languages (Lean 4, Idris, Agda) encode correctness invariants in type signatures. If LLM-generated code outputs include dependent type signatures, the type checker enforces correctness at generation time. Whether LLMs can generate dependently typed code with enforced invariants is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 20 functions with correctness invariants (sorted list guarantee, non-negative result, etc.). Ask LLMs to generate Lean 4 implementations where the return type encodes the invariant dependently (e.g., returning a Sorted type). Measure whether the type checker enforces the invariant without separate proof obligations.

**Why it matters:** If LLMs can encode safety invariants in dependent types, type checking becomes a lightweight, always-on correctness enforcement mechanism rather than a separate proof obligation. This could make formal verification more tractable.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4's type system is dependently typed. Using dependent types as inline proofs is idiomatic in Lean but not standard in LLM code generation. This is a novel application mode that could reduce proof overhead.

title: Importing Software Watermarking into Formally Verified Code: Detecting AI Provenance

original_idea.body:
# Importing Software Watermarking into Formally Verified Code: Detecting AI Provenance

**Problem:** AI-generated code is proliferating. Watermarking techniques from software provenance research could be adapted to formally verified code to detect AI provenance, but the interaction between watermarks and formal proofs is unstudied.

**Direction:** Implement a simple proof-invariant watermarking scheme for Lean 4 code (e.g., choosing equivalent proof steps with different tactic orderings to encode a bit pattern). Measure whether the watermark survives: (a) proof refactoring, (b) human editing, (c) extraction to executable. Test detectability.

**Why it matters:** If AI-generated formally verified code can be watermarked in a way that survives modification, it enables AI attribution in safety-critical code without breaking the formal proof. This has governance implications.

**Relevant context:** LLM output watermarking is an active research area (Kirchenbauer et al. 2023). Proof watermarking is novel. For governance of AI-generated safety-critical code, attribution matters.

title: Decomposing the Vericoding Pipeline: Which Stage (Spec→Proof→Execution) Is the Bottleneck?

original_idea.body:
# Decomposing the Vericoding Pipeline: Which Stage (Spec→Proof→Execution) Is the Bottleneck?

**Problem:** The end-to-end vericoding pipeline (natural language → formal spec → proof → executable code) fails at multiple stages. Whether spec generation, proof completion, or extraction to executable code is the primary bottleneck is not characterized.

**Direction:** Run 50 programs through the vericoding pipeline. At each stage, record success/failure: (1) spec generation (syntactically valid, semantically correct), (2) proof completion (proof compiles), (3) extraction (executable code runs correctly). Compute conditional probabilities across stages.

**Why it matters:** Knowing the bottleneck stage focuses research effort. If spec generation fails 60% of the time but proof completion fails 80% of the time conditional on correct spec, proof completion is the bottleneck. Resource allocation follows from this analysis.

**Relevant context:** VERINA (arXiv 2505.23135) decomposes verification into subtasks. ATLAS (POPL 2026) automates the full pipeline. A stage-by-stage bottleneck analysis has not been done across multiple LLMs.

title: Causal Intervention on Proof Hint Injection: At Which Proof Step Does Adding a Hint Most Help?

original_idea.body:
# Causal Intervention on Proof Hint Injection: At Which Proof Step Does Adding a Hint Most Help?

**Problem:** Lean 4 proofs can be guided by human-provided lemma hints (sorry placeholders, partial proofs). Where in the proof search process a hint has the most impact (early, middle, late) is not characterized.

**Direction:** Take 30 Lean 4 problems that LLMs fail to prove. Inject correct hints at different points: (a) first step only, (b) key lemma only, (c) last step only, (d) full proof scaffold. Measure which hint placement most reliably unlocks successful proof completion. Model as a causal graph.

**Why it matters:** Understanding where humans can most efficiently assist LLM proof search identifies the minimal human intervention required. If a single key lemma hint reduces failure rate by 50%, human-AI collaboration becomes much more tractable.

**Relevant context:** Lean 4's tactic system allows partial proofs (with sorry placeholders). The Self-Optimizing Trace Agent does not accept human hints. Human-in-the-loop formal verification is under-studied compared to fully automated approaches.

title: The Spec-to-Bug Causal Path: Does Spec Vagueness Cause Verifiably Insecure Code?
quick_reasoning: Addresses AI safety topic but scope is broad and direction could be more focused

original_idea.body:
# The Spec-to-Bug Causal Path: Does Spec Vagueness Cause Verifiably Insecure Code?

**Problem:** The causal chain from vague specification → underspecified formal spec → incomplete proof → undetected vulnerability has not been empirically measured end-to-end.

**Direction:** Take 20 programs with known vulnerabilities. Create both (a) precise natural language specs and (b) vague natural language specs. Run both through LLM vericoding pipelines. Measure whether vague specs produce formal proofs that miss the vulnerability. Measure end-to-end spec vagueness → vulnerability escape rate.

**Why it matters:** If spec vagueness is a primary causal factor in formal verification security failures, the intervention point is specification requirements — a governance and process issue, not just a technical one.

**Relevant context:** The spec quality problem is mentioned in ATLAS and VeriSpec papers but not causally linked to security outcomes. This closes the causal loop from spec quality to actual security.

title: Intervention at the Training Data Stage: Does Including Lean 4 Examples in SFT Data Improve Proof Generation?

original_idea.body:
# Intervention at the Training Data Stage: Does Including Lean 4 Examples in SFT Data Improve Proof Generation?

**Problem:** LLMs like Leanstral are fine-tuned on Lean 4 data. The causal link between training data composition (amount, quality, diversity of Lean 4 examples) and downstream proof generation success has not been established for open models.

**Direction:** Using Leanstral or a smaller open model, create training datasets with varying compositions: (a) 0 Lean examples, (b) 1K Lean examples from Mathlib, (c) 1K from VeriBench, (d) 1K from CSLib. Fine-tune and measure VeriBench performance per composition. Isolate the causal contribution of training domain.

**Why it matters:** If CSLib-domain training data is most effective for security-adjacent formal verification, this provides a concrete curriculum for training better safety-relevant verification models.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS generates 19K+ training examples. AlphaVerus bootstraps training data. The causal impact of specific data sources (especially CSLib vs. Mathlib) on proof generation for security applications is unknown.

title: Breaking the Human Review Bottleneck: Can LLM-Generated Proof Summaries Replace Line-by-Line Review?

original_idea.body:
# Breaking the Human Review Bottleneck: Can LLM-Generated Proof Summaries Replace Line-by-Line Review?

**Problem:** Human review of Lean 4 proofs is the primary bottleneck in deploying formally verified AI-generated code. Whether natural language proof summaries generated by LLMs are sufficient for human review is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 30 complete Lean 4 proofs. Have LLMs generate natural language summaries. Ask 10 CS students to: (a) approve/reject based on summary only, (b) approve/reject after reading full proof. Measure false approval rate per condition. Test whether summary-based review catches the same errors as full-proof review.

**Why it matters:** If LLM-generated summaries enable equally accurate human review in 10% of the time, the practical deployment bottleneck for formally verified AI code would be dramatically reduced.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code Security uses multi-stage verification to reduce false positives. Human review of formal proofs is mentioned as a bottleneck in multiple papers. The summary-as-review approach is unexplored.

title: Tracing the China-US Formal Verification Gap: A Benchmarked Comparison of Top Models
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Tracing the China-US Formal Verification Gap: A Benchmarked Comparison of Top Models

**Problem:** RAND's Sarma & Fisher (2026) report that China leads in AI-integrated theorem proving while US frontier labs have not prioritized this domain. This claim has not been empirically verified on standardized benchmarks.

**Direction:** Run VeriBench on available Chinese AI models with theorem proving capabilities (DeepSeek, ByteDance models) vs US frontier models (Claude, GPT-4, Gemini). Measure compilation rate, proof success rate, and failure mode distribution. Produce a structured comparison.

**Why it matters:** If the China-US gap is real and measurable, this supports RAND's policy recommendation for increased US investment in formal verification AI. If the gap is overstated, different policy priorities may be warranted.

**Relevant context:** RAND (February 2026) specifically calls out DeepSeek and ByteDance as leading in this domain. VeriBench provides a standardized evaluation platform. No published comparison exists.

title: Formal Verification as a Safety Assurance Floor: Success State Definition and Backward Gap Analysis

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification as a Safety Assurance Floor: Success State Definition and Backward Gap Analysis

**Problem:** Define a concrete success state: AI-generated Lean 4 code for security-critical systems achieves 95% formally verified correct specs with zero vacuous proofs and full edge-case coverage. Map the gaps from current state to this target.

**Direction:** Define a measurable success state for vericoding in security-critical applications. Then measure current performance on each dimension (compilation rate: ~60%, vacuity rate: unknown, edge case coverage: unknown). Compute the delta. Use gap analysis to prioritize which intervention would most advance toward the success state.

**Why it matters:** Without a defined success state, research effort is unfocused. The RAND report defines a goal (tipping cyber balance toward defense) but not measurable technical milestones. This operationalizes that goal.

**Relevant context:** RAND (2026) defines a strategic success state but not technical metrics. VeriBench provides partial metrics. This is a structured gap analysis between current capability and deployment-ready formal verification.

title: From Vibe Coding to Vericoding: What Infrastructure Is Missing for Mainstream Adoption?

original_idea.body:
# From Vibe Coding to Vericoding: What Infrastructure Is Missing for Mainstream Adoption?

**Problem:** The community has defined the goal of replacing vibe coding (unverified AI code) with vericoding (formally verified AI code). The specific infrastructure gaps blocking mainstream adoption are not systematically mapped.

**Direction:** Survey 20 software developers on: what would make formal verification of AI-generated code practical for their workflow? Complement with a technical gap analysis: spec writing tools, proof debugging, proof maintenance, compute cost, language coverage. Prioritize gaps by impact × feasibility.

**Why it matters:** Knowing the actual adoption blockers directs research toward what would make the largest practical difference. Without this mapping, researchers optimize technically interesting problems that may not remove the adoption blockers.

**Relevant context:** The vericoding concept (POPL 2026) defines the goal. ATLAS, AlphaVerus, CSLib address technical components. The adoption infrastructure gap analysis has not been done. This is analogous to the role of user studies in HCI research.

title: Backward Engineering a Safety Case for AI-Generated Cryptographic Code

original_idea.body:
# Backward Engineering a Safety Case for AI-Generated Cryptographic Code

**Problem:** Define success: a complete formal safety case for AI-generated AES-256 implementation. Work backward to identify what formal specifications, proof obligations, and verification tools are minimally necessary.

**Direction:** Write a complete safety case argument structure for an AI-generated AES-256 implementation. Identify each assurance claim and the formal proof required to discharge it. Attempt to generate those proofs using Lean 4/Dafny. Measure which claims are provable today vs. which require future tool development.

**Why it matters:** Cryptographic implementations are the highest-stakes target for formally verified code. A complete safety case study reveals exactly which formal methods tools are missing and which are ready to deploy.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS pipeline generates verified Dafny programs including cryptographic examples. CSLib roadmap does not include cryptographic algorithms. RAND benchmarks include cryptographic implementations. This is a concrete backward engineering exercise.

title: Defining Done for CSLib: What Would a Complete Formally Verified Undergraduate CS Curriculum Look Like?

original_idea.body:
# Defining Done for CSLib: What Would a Complete Formally Verified Undergraduate CS Curriculum Look Like?

**Problem:** CSLib aims to cover undergraduate algorithms and data structures by 2026. The definition of 'complete' (how many algorithms, which edge cases, which security-relevant variants) is underspecified.

**Direction:** Survey 5 undergraduate CS curricula. Extract the complete list of algorithms and data structures taught. Compare against current CSLib coverage. Define a precise specification of 'complete CSLib' including security-relevant variants. Measure current coverage percentage as a baseline.

**Why it matters:** A precise definition of completion enables tracking CSLib progress and identifies whether AI assistance can accelerate the timeline. Without a definition, 'complete CSLib' is not a measurable goal.

**Relevant context:** CSLib paper (arXiv 2602.04846) describes 2026 roadmap at a high level. No precise specification of what constitutes undergraduate-level coverage exists. This is foundational planning work.

title: Working Backward from Verified AI Model Evaluation: What Would Cryptographic Proof of AI Evaluation Require?

original_idea.body:
# Working Backward from Verified AI Model Evaluation: What Would Cryptographic Proof of AI Evaluation Require?

**Problem:** RAND's Sarma & Fisher (2026) propose using formal methods to cryptographically prove AI models underwent approved evaluations without tampering — enabling credible verification in international AI governance agreements. The technical requirements for this are undefined.

**Direction:** Define a minimal technical stack for a 'verified AI evaluation protocol': (1) formal specification of evaluation procedure, (2) cryptographic commitment to model weights, (3) proof of evaluation execution. Identify each technical component's current readiness level. Estimate which components are 10-year vs. 2-year problems.

**Why it matters:** This is a critical governance application of formal methods to AI safety. If the technical components exist, deployment planning can begin. If they do not, early-stage research can be motivated by this concrete goal.

**Relevant context:** RAND (2026) proposes this as a future direction. Zero-knowledge proofs (SNARKs, STARKs) could provide the cryptographic component. Lean 4 could provide the formal specification. No synthesis of these components has been proposed.

title: Success State for Lean 4 HumanEval: What Would 95% Compilation Rate Require?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Success State for Lean 4 HumanEval: What Would 95% Compilation Rate Require?

**Problem:** Define a success state of 95% Lean 4 HumanEval compilation rate. Work backward to identify: what training data, prompting improvements, and architecture changes are each contributing an expected X% improvement?

**Direction:** Analyze the error distribution in current Lean 4 HumanEval failures across 3 models. For each error class, estimate the maximum improvement achievable through: (a) better prompting, (b) more training data, (c) architectural improvements. Build a simple additive contribution model. Identify the highest-leverage intervention.

**Why it matters:** 95% compilation rate is the threshold at which Lean 4 proof generation would become practically usable for most software verification tasks. Understanding the path from 60% to 95% directs research investment.

**Relevant context:** Self-Optimizing Trace Agent achieves ~60%. VeriBench provides baseline error analysis. This backcasting approach is used in roadmapping but has not been applied to formal verification capability improvement.

title: Proof Generation Failure × Model Homogeneity: Do All LLMs Fail on the Same Lean 4 Problems?

original_idea.body:
# Proof Generation Failure × Model Homogeneity: Do All LLMs Fail on the Same Lean 4 Problems?

**Problem:** If multiple LLMs fail on the same Lean 4 problems, a single LLM ensemble is unlikely to solve them. The overlap between different models' failure sets would indicate whether diverse ensembles can close the gap.

**Direction:** Run 5 LLMs on all VeriBench tasks. Compute Jaccard similarity of their failure sets. Identify problems that all models fail (irreducible hard set) vs. problems where at least one model succeeds (coverage-improvable set). Measure what fraction of failures could be solved by an oracle ensemble.

**Why it matters:** High overlap in failure sets would indicate systematic reasoning gaps common to all current LLMs — a genuine AI safety concern suggesting model homogeneity risks. Low overlap would indicate ensemble strategies are a viable path to near-term improvement.

**Relevant context:** AI homogeneity as a risk (from previous idea generation) applies here: if all LLMs have the same formal reasoning blind spots, the safety signal from any single model is correlated with all others. This compounds the risk.

title: Vague Spec × Vulnerable Code: Compounding Failure When Specification and Implementation Both Come from the Same LLM
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Vague Spec × Vulnerable Code: Compounding Failure When Specification and Implementation Both Come from the Same LLM

**Problem:** When the same LLM generates both the formal specification and the implementation, systematic biases (same omissions, same incorrect assumptions) may propagate across both, causing proofs to pass while missing the same class of vulnerabilities.

**Direction:** Compare two conditions on 30 security-critical programs: (a) spec and implementation generated by the same LLM, (b) spec generated by one LLM and implementation by a different LLM. Measure whether cross-model pairs catch more vulnerabilities in subsequent analysis. Test statistical significance.

**Why it matters:** Self-verification is a known limitation in AI safety. If same-model spec+implementation pairs produce correlated blind spots, all-in-one vericoding pipelines are systematically overconfident. Cross-model diversity would be required for safety-critical applications.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code Security's self-reflection step uses the same model that generated the code. AlphaVerus uses translation between languages (Dafny→Verus) which may introduce cross-model diversity. The compounding risk of correlated spec+implementation failures is not studied.

title: Hallucination × Formal Proof: When Confident Wrong Proofs Fool Non-Expert Reviewers
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped to specific AI safety failure mode with clear measurement methodology

original_idea.body:
# Hallucination × Formal Proof: When Confident Wrong Proofs Fool Non-Expert Reviewers

**Problem:** LLMs hallucinate confidently. In formal verification, a confident but wrong proof (that fails Lean's checker) would be caught. But a confident wrong specification might pass all automated checks while missing the intended safety property. Non-expert reviewers may not catch this.

**Direction:** Generate 20 formally verified programs where the spec is subtly wrong (verified but missing a key safety property). Present to 15 CS students for review with 5 minutes per program. Measure false approval rate. Compare to a condition where the correct spec is provided. Test whether confidence language in LLM output affects approval rate.

**Why it matters:** If non-expert reviewers of LLM-generated formal specs systematically approve subtly wrong specs (especially when the LLM expresses high confidence), formal verification provides a false safety guarantee that may be worse than no verification.

**Relevant context:** AI sycophancy research shows LLM outputs influence human judgment. Formal verification is being positioned as an accessible safety tool for non-experts. The compounding risk of LLM hallucination and non-expert review is not studied in this context.

title: Benchmark Gaming × Safety Signal: If LLMs Overfit to Lean Benchmarks, Can They Still Verify Novel Code?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI safety problem in formal verification with concrete experimental approach

original_idea.body:
# Benchmark Gaming × Safety Signal: If LLMs Overfit to Lean Benchmarks, Can They Still Verify Novel Code?

**Problem:** If LLMs improve on Lean 4 benchmarks through benchmark-specific optimization (few-shot memorization, dataset leakage) rather than genuine formal reasoning, the safety signal from benchmark performance would be misleading. Compounding this with deployment of such models in safety-critical verification creates a dangerous situation.

**Direction:** Train a lightweight model variant on VeriBench training examples (benchmark-specific SFT). Compare its performance on VeriBench vs. on a held-out set of novel Lean 4 tasks created after the benchmark. Measure generalization gap. Determine whether the VeriBench score overstates actual formal reasoning capability.

**Why it matters:** If state-of-the-art Lean 4 performance is partially explained by benchmark overfitting, safety decisions based on these scores (e.g., deploying AI-assisted formal verification in critical systems) rest on inflated capability estimates.

**Relevant context:** Benchmark contamination is documented in NLP. VeriBench is publicly available since ICML 2025. The compounding risk of overfitting and safety-critical deployment has not been studied for formal verification benchmarks specifically.

title: Legacy Code × Formal Verification: Can AI Generate Lean 4 Specs for Code Without Documentation?

original_idea.body:
# Legacy Code × Formal Verification: Can AI Generate Lean 4 Specs for Code Without Documentation?

**Problem:** Much security-critical legacy code has no documentation or specifications. Whether LLMs can reverse-engineer formal specifications from undocumented legacy code — a necessary step for formally verifying legacy systems — is unstudied.

**Direction:** Take 30 well-known open-source C functions with no inline documentation. Have LLMs: (1) generate natural language descriptions, (2) convert to Lean 4 formal specs, (3) complete proofs. Compare generated specs to expert-written gold specs. Measure accuracy without any documentation as input.

**Why it matters:** The RAND report specifically mentions converting legacy code as a key application of formal methods. If AI cannot handle undocumented code, the most important safety target (legacy critical infrastructure) remains unreachable.

**Relevant context:** RAND (2026) lists converting legacy code to memory-safe languages as a benchmark target. Claude Code Security analyzed undocumented production codebases. The interaction of legacy code's lack of spec and formal verification requirements is a specific gap.

title: Formally Verified Code × AI Model Tampering: Can Formal Methods Verify Model Evaluation Integrity?

original_idea.body:
# Formally Verified Code × AI Model Tampering: Can Formal Methods Verify Model Evaluation Integrity?

**Problem:** RAND proposes using formal methods to verify AI model evaluations without tampering. A compounding risk: if the verification framework itself uses AI to generate proofs, those AI components could be tampered with, undermining the integrity guarantee.

**Direction:** Design a minimal threat model for a tamper-evident AI evaluation verification system. Identify which components must be formally verified by humans vs. which could be AI-assisted. Test whether a Lean 4 proof of a simple evaluation protocol can be generated, reviewed, and validated without AI in the critical path.

**Why it matters:** An AI-generated proof of AI evaluation integrity creates a circular dependency. If the proof generator is the AI being evaluated, the safety case collapses. This is a foundational governance design question.

**Relevant context:** RAND (2026) proposes cryptographic proof of AI evaluations. Zero-knowledge proofs (SNARKs) could provide non-AI-dependent verification. The circular dependency between AI formal verification tools and AI governance applications is an unexplored compounding risk.

title: LLM Calibration for Lean 4 Proofs: Is Stated Confidence Correlated with Proof Success?

original_idea.body:
# LLM Calibration for Lean 4 Proofs: Is Stated Confidence Correlated with Proof Success?

**Problem:** LLMs can be asked to express confidence in their Lean 4 proofs before submitting. Whether this expressed confidence is calibrated (higher confidence predicts higher success rate) is unknown and has safety implications.

**Direction:** Run 80 VeriBench tasks. For each task, ask the LLM to express confidence (0-10) that its proof will compile, then submit the proof. Measure calibration: plot confidence vs. actual compilation rate. Compute Expected Calibration Error. Test across 3 models.

**Why it matters:** If LLMs are poorly calibrated on formal proofs, expressed confidence cannot be used as a filter or triage signal. Calibration is a key safety property for human-AI collaboration in verification workflows.

**Relevant context:** LLM calibration is studied for factual claims and code generation, but not for formal proof generation. Given that proof success is binary and verifiable, this is an ideal domain for calibration measurement.

title: Formal Verification of AI Agent Tool Calls: Can Lean 4 Specify Safe Tool-Call Sequences?

original_idea.body:
# Formal Verification of AI Agent Tool Calls: Can Lean 4 Specify Safe Tool-Call Sequences?

**Problem:** AI agents executing tool calls (file I/O, network, code execution) can cause irreversible harm. Whether Lean 4 formal specifications can express and verify safety properties of tool-call sequences (e.g., 'never delete a file without prior confirmation') is unexplored.

**Direction:** Model 10 AI agent scenarios as state machines. Write Lean 4 specifications for safety properties (reachability, invariants, forbidden states). Attempt to prove these properties using Lean 4. Measure which agent safety properties are expressible and provable in Lean 4's type theory.

**Why it matters:** If formal methods can verify AI agent safety properties at the specification level, this provides a rigorous complement to runtime guardrails. This connects the formal verification field directly to AI agent safety.

**Relevant context:** Claude Code (Anthropic) executes tools with significant system access. Lean 4's dependent types can express state machine properties. No work applies formal specification to AI agent tool-call safety.

title: The Proof Size Problem: Are LLM-Generated Lean 4 Proofs Unnecessarily Long?

original_idea.body:
# The Proof Size Problem: Are LLM-Generated Lean 4 Proofs Unnecessarily Long?

**Problem:** LLM-generated Lean 4 proofs may be systematically longer than necessary (redundant lemmas, unnecessary case splits). Proof size correlates with maintainability and readability, both safety-relevant for long-term code maintenance.

**Direction:** For 30 problems where LLMs generate working Lean 4 proofs, measure proof length (lines of code, number of tactics, lemma count). Compare to reference (shortest known) proofs. Compute size inflation factor. Test whether shorter prompting strategies reduce proof size.

**Why it matters:** Excessively long proofs are harder for humans to review, increasing the probability of undetected errors. Proof minimization is a safety engineering concern that is not addressed by current benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** Human-written Lean proofs tend to be more concise than LLM-generated ones (observed qualitatively in Mathlib contributions). No quantitative study of LLM proof verbosity vs. human expert proofs exists.

title: Multi-Step Proof Planning vs. Tactic-by-Tactic Generation: Which Architecture Succeeds More on Lean 4?

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Step Proof Planning vs. Tactic-by-Tactic Generation: Which Architecture Succeeds More on Lean 4?

**Problem:** LLMs can generate Lean 4 proofs either by planning the full proof structure first then filling details, or by generating tactic by tactic. Whether planning-first architecture outperforms tactic-sequential generation on VeriBench is not tested.

**Direction:** Implement two Lean 4 proof generation architectures: (a) plan-then-fill (generate proof outline with sorry placeholders, then fill each sorry), (b) sequential tactic generation (standard left-to-right). Run both on 50 VeriBench tasks. Measure compilation rate and iterations required.

**Why it matters:** Identifying the superior proof generation architecture is a prerequisite for building better verification tools. Proof planning mirrors how human Lean experts work — if it helps LLMs, it suggests a path to human-level formal reasoning.

**Relevant context:** Chain-of-thought prompting (planning) improves LLM reasoning across domains. For Lean 4, planning-first is used informally but not systematically compared to sequential generation. This is a concrete architectural experiment.

title: CSLib Completion Acceleration: Does AI Assistance Measurably Speed Up New CSLib Theorem Additions?

original_idea.body:
# CSLib Completion Acceleration: Does AI Assistance Measurably Speed Up New CSLib Theorem Additions?

**Problem:** CSLib is being developed manually. Whether AI assistance (LLM-generated proof drafts reviewed by humans) measurably accelerates CSLib theorem entry development vs. human-only development is untested.

**Direction:** Recruit 6 graduate students for a within-subject experiment. Each adds 5 new CSLib-style theorems to Lean 4: (a) fully manually, (b) using LLM-generated proof drafts. Measure time, number of Lean compiler errors, and final proof quality. Compare conditions.

**Why it matters:** CSLib is a key building block for the safe AI code ecosystem. If AI assistance halves development time, the 2026 target is achievable. If AI-generated drafts require so much correction that they offer no speedup, different development strategies are needed.

**Relevant context:** CSLib roadmap (arXiv 2602.04846) has concrete 2026 milestones. Mistral Leanstral and similar tools exist. No experiment measures AI-assisted CSLib development productivity. This is a direct test of AI assistance value for a safety-critical infrastructure project.

title: Natural Language Spec Precision and Proof Success: Measuring the Correlation

original_idea.body:
# Natural Language Spec Precision and Proof Success: Measuring the Correlation

**Problem:** Formal proof success likely depends on the precision of natural language input specifications. Whether more precise natural language specs lead to higher LLM proof success rates — and by how much — is not quantified.

**Direction:** Take 25 VeriBench problems. Create 3 natural language specification variants per problem: (a) minimal (docstring only), (b) medium (docstring + examples), (c) maximum (docstring + examples + edge cases + invariants). Run the same LLM on all 75 inputs. Measure compilation rate per spec level.

**Why it matters:** If spec precision is a strong predictor of proof success, the intervention is clear: improve input spec quality. This would motivate spec-elicitation tools as a component of safe AI code generation pipelines.

**Relevant context:** ATLAS generates specs from examples. AlphaVerus starts from Dafny specs. VeriBench uses consistent problem descriptions. Spec precision as an independent variable has not been systematically tested.
